messages.text: I lead a regional nonprofit newsroom. A large video platform has approached us with an offer to feature our weekly local-investigations program, promising guaranteed revenue for the first year. The potential reach is massive, as it would put our work in front of people who never visit our site. However, they want early access, a specific format, and the right to use their recommendation system to promote clips. Our membership growth has hit a wall, so the funding and audience are tempting, but my editors are deeply worried that we'll end up chasing stories that fit the platform's preference rather than our own investigative goals.

It is essential to decouple distribution, financing, format, data, and editorial authority. A guaranteed year can certainly fund your work, but it will fundamentally change which stories get visibility and rewards. You need to ask what the platform can reject, edit, title, clip, delay, or demonetize, as well as what audience data you will actually receive and what happens to your program or subscribers once that guarantee expires. Weigh those answers against the current cost of operating with a smaller audience.

The platform claims they won't approve topics or scripts, provided we follow their general policies. They are insisting on a format between eighteen and twenty-two minutes. We would retain control of the full version and could publish it on our own site one day after they post it. My video editor actually thinks the format discipline might sharpen our storytelling, but I’m struggling to distinguish between helpful production constraints and actual editorial capture.

Format can be a useful craft constraint, but the line to editorial capture is crossed when platform rules, promotion, or revenue models start dictating which investigations survive. Request their full policy and the specific appeal process for disputes. Retain your right to publish any compliant full report on your own channels, and ensure you track any work that gets altered or abandoned solely to meet their format requirements. The one-day publishing delay is less critical than ensuring your audience relationship remains portable.

They said we'd get views, watch time, broad geography, and referral totals, but no subscriber contact info due to privacy rules. They will allow us to prompt viewers to join our newsletter, though they noted external links might not be prominent on every device. The guarantee covers production costs and part of a reporter's salary, but after year one, the money is entirely view-dependent.

The guarantee is essentially funding an experiment, but the post-guarantee model creates a completely different set of editorial incentives. You should model the second year without assuming high audience conversion rates and decide now what you refuse to change just to chase view-based revenue. Test that newsletter path on various devices, and consider their followers as rented reach, not as members you can reliably contact.

Our investigations editor suggested a pilot of six episodes before committing to a full season. The platform, however, wants a twelve-episode season and says promotion will be weak if we don't commit to consistency. They won't specify how much promotion we get or where episodes appear because their recommendations change. We could negotiate an exit after six, but the guarantee would be slashed by more than half.

They are effectively asking you to trade a commitment for an undefined benefit. A six-episode exit reduces your duration, but it might leave the test inconclusive if promotion is tied to the full twelve. Instead of chasing an algorithmic promise they can't define, ask for minimum deliverables they can control—like specific placement, marketing support, or technical assistance. Ensure the decision remains viable on the guaranteed revenue alone, even if the exposure turns out to be modest.

They offered two homepage placements and a named partner manager, but still no recommendation volume guarantees. If the agreement ends, we can remove our archive, though clips shared by users might persist. The contract also lets them use short excerpts to promote the service for three years. Our lawyer is reviewing that, so I don't know yet if we can limit the contexts or attach our branding.

Those reuse terms are not just a legal appendix; they directly affect your long-term reputation and control. Don't make a decision until you have clarity on the permitted contexts, duration, attribution, and removal rights. The two placements are a concrete offer, whereas the recommendation volume is just an upside scenario. Wait for the revised draft rather than relying on their verbal description.

My board chair wants an answer in principle before our next meeting because the platform is finalizing its autumn slate. I could say we’re interested, subject to rights and editorial protections, but my editors fear even a public expression of interest creates irreversible momentum. Yet, if I don't signal interest, we might lose the slot entirely. We also haven't agreed on what second-year economics would be unacceptable.

An expression of interest should explicitly name the unresolved conditions and avoid any public announcement of the program. Internally, you need to define your minimum rights, acceptable first-year commitment, and a clear 'walk-away' rule for the second year before the timeline forces your hand. Ask the platform for a short written hold while the legal review is ongoing. If they refuse, the cost of that urgency is a factor you should include in your assessment.

My position is to send a private, nonbinding statement of interest conditioned on acceptable excerpt rights, source protection, our ability to publish every full report, and an exit structure the editors support. I won't seek board approval until the lawyer returns the draft and we model year two without guaranteed revenue. We still need to decide if twelve episodes are worth the attention they'll pull from our existing reporting.

That position keeps the door open without treating uncertain promotion or unresolved rights as settled value. The next step depends on the revised contract, a conservative post-guarantee model, and a real comparison of the opportunity costs. Keep things quiet externally until those inputs are in hand. Your goal now is to resolve conditions, not to force a decision on a proposal that is still fundamentally incomplete.

The lawyer returned the draft. The platform will limit promotional excerpt rights to the contract term plus one year and will attach our branding, but they want to keep already-produced compilations online afterward. They also say we can withhold excerpts that endanger a confidential source, provided we explain the concern to their legal team. My investigations editor is worried that even explaining the concern might reveal too much.

Source protection should never depend on persuading an external legal team with sensitive details. You should seek a newsroom-controlled designation for source-risk material, perhaps with a narrow dispute process that doesn't require revealing identities. Define whether old compilations can remain after the episode is pulled and whether the context can be updated. This is progress, but the exception mechanism is still the crux of your editorial control.

Editors mapped the twelve episodes against our calendar. Doing this will delay two investigations unless we hire a freelance producer, which the guarantee can cover. One of those delayed investigations involves municipal contracting and is time-sensitive. The platform format could make that reporting accessible to a much larger local audience, though. It’s not just 'platform work' versus 'serious work'—it’s more nuanced than that.

Build the season starting with your editorial priorities, then test which stories fit without distortion. Protect those time-sensitive investigations at all costs and price the freelance help honestly. You need to track which stories are accelerated, delayed, or declined because of this partnership. The evaluation should focus on what reporting you gained or lost, not on the assumption that video is inherently less serious.

Our community advisory group was split. Younger members said our site is effectively invisible to many people and warned that independence without reach is just self-congratulation. Others worried the platform's culture rewards outrage and might scare off local sources. They suggested every episode should have a permanent page on our site with documents, corrections, and contact info.

Creating a permanent owned page is a great way to turn rented reach into an accountable record. Require the platform to link there, publish your source documents and corrections under your own standards, and measure conversion without viewing it as the only metric. Plan your moderation and subject communication carefully; distribution changes the environment even if the journalism remains the same.

The platform gave me two more weeks but wants to list us publicly among prospective autumn partners before our board vote. They say it’s not a commitment and helps their sales team. I declined, because a public signal would be hard to reverse. My board chair thinks I might be making the negotiation harder to protect against momentum, but I want the board to decide before our name is attached to their story.

Declining the announcement definitely has a negotiation cost, but record that cost rather than assuming it was a mistake. Ask if they can hold the capacity privately while you vote, and what they would withdraw if they can't publicize the relationship. That answer will clarify whether early signaling is just incidental planning or a key part of the value they're seeking from you.

I’m still not asking the board to approve. I’ll return only when the source-risk exception is newsroom-controlled, the owned episode pages are confirmed, and we have a budget that protects the time-sensitive investigation. The second-year model will assume no guaranteed revenue. We’re interested, but an autumn slot and a better excerpt term aren't enough to decide if this is a controlled experiment or the start of a dependency we haven't priced.

Your current position is a disciplined continuation of the negotiation, not indecision. You've successfully narrowed the reuse rights, identified a source-protection boundary, and made the opportunity costs concrete. Hold onto the draft changes, the calendar comparisons, the community feedback, and the conservative model. The board can decide once these conditions are met; until then, a recommendation would rely on too many undefined variables.
